title: MokA: Multimodal Low-Rank Adaptation for MLLMs

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The discussion states 'This work completely solves the problem of multimodal adaptation in large language models' and 'MokA's novel low-rank decomposition with cross-attention absolutely ensures superior model performance and sets a new standard... This definitive advancement paves the way for final, conclusive exploration.' These absolute, unqualified claims directly contradict the abstract's own hedged statement that 'gains vary among backbones and modalities, suggesting further exploration is needed to fully assess its generality and robustness,' and are unsupported by the mixed experimental results (e.g., Table 3 shows MokA is not the best method for LLaMA2 on speech-text benchmarks).

The text states 'we proudly propose MokA, a unique and superior fine-tuning strategy tailored for MLLMs. MokA boldly guarantees both unimodal preservation and enhanced cross-modal interaction, delivering an unmatched, targeted solution that redefines efficient and effective multimodal adaptation.' This promotional, absolute language ('guarantees', 'unmatched') is inconsistent with the paper's own acknowledgment in the abstract that improvements vary and further exploration is needed, and is not an appropriate or accurate characterization for a related-work comparison section.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1, discussion of Qwen2.5-VL vs. Table 1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims 'Qwen2.5-VL with LoRA outperforms both LLaMA-2 and Qwen2 under the LoRA fine-tuning setting.' However, Table 1 shows Qwen2.5-VL LoRA scores 73.00 (MUSIC-AVQA)/71.38 (AVE), while LLaMA2 LoRA scores 73.41/69.84 and Qwen2 LoRA scores 72.83/72.13. Qwen2.5-VL does NOT outperform LLaMA2 on MUSIC-AVQA (73.00 < 73.41) nor outperform Qwen2 on AVE (71.38 < 72.13), contradicting the stated claim.

Table 2 reports LLaMA2 LoRA's MME score as 90.85, but Table 4 (which compiles the same LoRA/LLaMA2 results) reports the MME score as 908.52 for the identical method and benchmark. These two values for the same experiment are inconsistent by an order of magnitude.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 5 vs. Table 3 (Multiple LoRA, AIR-Bench, LLaMA2)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 5 reports 'Multiple LoRA' AIR-Bench score as 31.97, while Table 3 reports the same method/backbone/benchmark (LLaMA2, AIR-Bench) score as 32.80. These values are inconsistent for what should be the same experimental result.

Table 5 reports MokA's AIR-Bench score as 39.64, while Table 3 reports MokA's AIR-Bench score (LLaMA2) as 36.70 for what should be the identical experimental configuration. This is a substantial numerical discrepancy (39.64 vs 36.70) for the same method/backbone/benchmark combination.

The text states 'our method achieves stable and consistent performance gains across multiple benchmark datasets, further confirming its effectiveness.' However, Table 3 shows that for LLaMA2, MokA's MMAU score (35.40) is lower than both Uni-modal LoRA (36.80) and Uni LoRA + MM LoRA (37.10), and MokA's AIR-Bench score (36.70) is lower than Uni LoRA + MM LoRA (37.60). This contradicts the claim of consistent gains, as MokA is outperformed by two baselines in this setting.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B, Equations (14)-(15) vs. main text Equations (5)-(6)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In the main text, the cross-attention scaling factor is sqrt(d), with d defined as 'the dimensionality of the projected token embeddings' (Section 2.2.2, Eq. 5-6). In Appendix B, the identical attention equations are rewritten with the denominator sqrt(N_t), where N_t is the number of text tokens, not an embedding dimension. Using the sequence length instead of the key/channel dimension for attention scaling is mathematically inconsistent with standard scaled dot-product attention and contradicts the main text's own formula for the same operation.

Table 6 reports MokA's 'Avg. forward time per sample' as 1.134x while also reporting POPE Acc (a visual-text/VL benchmark metric) in the same row. However, Table 8 shows that for the VL setting (MME_percep), MokA's forward time is 1.069x, while the 1.134x figure actually corresponds to the AVL (MUSIC-AVQA, audio-visual-text) setting. This suggests Table 6 mismatches performance (from the visual-text/POPE setting) with efficiency metrics (from the audio-visual-text/AVL setting).

The diagrams for 'Uni LoRA + MM LoRA' and 'Uni LoRA + MM LoRA + Gate' show a sequential flow 'Shared B --> Multimodal B --> Multimodal A' (and with Gate inserted mid-sequence), which is backwards relative to how LoRA modules operate (input should pass through matrix A first, then B) and inconsistent with the textual description of these baselines as having a unimodal A/B branch plus a separate, parallel shared multimodal LoRA branch, not a serial B-B-A pathway.
